title: How many people are in your family?
goal: Talk about your family and ages with 有 and 沒有 — and accept that in Mandarin "brother" and "sister" are not one word each but two.
bekal: use 有 for having and negate it ONLY with 沒有
name family members with the right word for age and side of the family
ask and give ages in three different forms

dialogs.title: 對話 — 看照片
dialogs.intro: In the dorm dining room, Xiaomei sees a family photo on Budi's phone.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: Is this your family? So many people!
lines.literal: this — is — you — home-people — (question)? very — many — people — (wow)!

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Yes. There are six of us.
lines.literal: right. I — home — have — six — (measure word) — people.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: Wow! Do you have brothers and sisters?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [有|Yǒu]。[一個|Yí ge][哥哥|gēge]，[兩個|liǎng ge][妹妹|mèimei]。
lines.id: Yes. One older brother and two younger sisters.
lines.literal: have. one — (measure word) — older-brother, two — (measure word) — younger-sister.

lines.text: [你|Nǐ][哥哥|gēge][幾歲|jǐ suì]？[不對|Bú duì]…[多大|duō dà]？
lines.id: How old is your brother? Oops — I mean, how old is he?
lines.literal: you — older-brother — how-many — years? not — right… how — big?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [他|Tā][二十八歲|èrshíbā suì]。[他|Tā][已經|yǐjīng][結婚|jiéhūn][了|le]。
lines.literal: he — twenty-eight — years. he — already — tie-marriage — (now).

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [有|Yǒu][一個|yí ge][女兒|nǚ'ér]，[兩歲|liǎng suì]。[超|Chāo][可愛|kě'ài]！
lines.id: One daughter, two years old. Super cute!
lines.literal: have — one — (measure word) — female-child, two — years. super — can-be-loved!

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [對啊|Duì a]！[妳|Nǐ][呢|ne]？[妳|Nǐ][家|jiā][有|yǒu][幾個|jǐ ge][人|rén]？
lines.id: That's right! And you? How many in your family?
lines.literal: right — (wow)! you — (what about)? you — home — have — how-many — (measure word) — people?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.literal: three — (measure word). dad, mom — and — I.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [妳|Nǐ][沒有|méi yǒu][兄弟姐妹|xiōngdì jiěmèi][嗎|ma]？
lines.id: You don't have any brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: No. That's very common in Taiwan.
lines.literal: not — have. at — Taiwan, this — very — common-widespread.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: Then your parents must really dote on you.
lines.literal: then — you — father-mother — surely — very — dote-on — you.

lines.text: [太疼了|Tài téng le]！[所以|Suǒyǐ][我|wǒ][還|hái][住|zhù][家裡|jiālǐ][啊|a]！
lines.id: Way too much! That's why I still live at home!
lines.literal: too — dote-on — (now)! so — I — still — live — home-inside — (wow)!

notes: ⚠️ **口 is a special measure word for family members** and is used for nothing else. *我家有六口人* sounds warm and traditional; *六個人* is also correct and just as common among young people.

⚠️ **幾歲 is only for small children.** Asking an adult's age with 幾歲 sounds like talking to a kindergartner. For people your own age use **多大**, for much older people use **您貴庚** (*nín guìgēng*) — and safest of all, don't ask.
**The 了 in 結婚了 and 我是叔叔了 is not a past tense** but a marker of **change of state**: not before, now yes. Unit 11 covers it fully; for now, just get a feel for the pattern.
**超 (*chāo*, "super") is young Taiwanese slang** that replaces 很: 超可愛, 超好吃, 超累. It's casual and everywhere, but don't use it in formal writing.
⚠️ **疼 means "to dote on" when it's about people, and "to hurt" when it's about the body.** *我媽媽很疼我* (my mom dotes on me) vs *我頭很疼* (my head hurts). Context always separates them.

grammars.title: ⚠️ 有 is negated ONLY with 沒, never with 不
body: Mandarin has two negative words, and the split is simple but rigid: **不** for almost every verb, **沒** for 有 and for things that didn't happen. No exceptions.
after: **沒有 can be shortened to 沒** before another verb: *我沒去* (I didn't go). But when it negates 有 itself, it usually stays whole: *我沒有錢*.
⚠️ Compare the last two rows once more. **不 negates habits or will; 沒 negates events.** *我不吃豬肉* = I don't eat pork (a principle). *我沒吃* = I haven't eaten (a fact about today).

grammars.title: Age: three forms, three levels of politeness
body: Mandarin picks the question word for age depending on who is being asked. Using the wrong one isn't a grammar mistake, but it sounds off at once.

head: Question
Pīnyīn
Asking
Answer
rows: students — asks the year of study, not age

after: ⚠️ **Giving your age doesn't need 是**: *我二十歲* — not *我是二十歲*. Number + 歲 already works like an adjective, and adjectives don't take 是. This is the first taste of a rule unit 14 covers in full.
**大一, 大二, 大三, 大四** are years at university (first to fourth year) — short for 大學一年級. Asking *你大幾？* is the most natural way for students in Taiwan to get acquainted.

sections.title: ⚠️ Family: "brother" and "sister" each split in two

blocks.text: English marks brother vs. sister but not older vs. younger — you add "big" or "little" if it matters. Mandarin **builds both into the word itself**, and has no single-character word for "sibling".

⚠️ The full system is far more complex — Mandarin has different words for uncles on the father's and the mother's side, and for those older and younger than your father. At A1, the first ten rows are enough. **外 ("outside") in 外公 and 外婆 marks the mother's side**, a relic of the days when children were considered part of the father's family.

blocks.title: 阿姨 and 叔叔 are also for strangers
items: In Taiwan, children call any woman their mother's age **阿姨** and any man their father's age **叔叔**, even if they're not related at all.
Adults call much older people **阿伯** (*ābó*, "uncle", for an older man) and **阿姨** or **阿嬤** (*āmà*, from Hokkien, "grandma").
⚠️ Calling an older waitress **阿姨** sounds warm; calling her **小姐** sounds cold.
**帥哥** (*shuàigē*, "handsome") and **美女** (*měinǚ*, "beautiful") are what night-market sellers call any customer. It's not flirting — just a friendly greeting.

sections.title: 有 and 沒有 in everyday use

blocks.text: ⚠️ **有一點 always introduces something unpleasant**: 有一點貴 (a bit pricey), 有一點累 (a bit tired), 有一點吵 (a bit noisy). For pleasant things, people use 一點 without 有, or a different word: *便宜一點* (a little cheaper). The mistake *有一點好* sounds strange to Taiwanese ears.
